claim: Transient testosterone pulses (T-pulses) in males after social encounters can alter their spatial distribution on a territory.
source: We tested the novel concept that the rewarding effects of transient testosterone pulses (T-pulses) in males after social encounters alter their spatial distribution on a territory.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested in the study, supported by experimental data showing males spent more time at the nest after T-injections.

claim: In free-living monogamous California mice, males administered three T-injections at the nest spent more time at the nest than males treated with placebo injections.
source: In free-living monogamous California mice (Peromyscus californicus), males administered three T-injections at the nest spent more time at the nest than males treated with placebo injections.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: T-induced place preferences in the laboratory are mimicked by T-injections in the field.
source: This mimics T-induced place preferences in the laboratory.
evidence: This claim draws on previous laboratory studies and compares them to the current field results.

claim: Female mates of T-treated males spent less time at the nest.
source: Female mates of T-treated males spent less time at the nest but the pair produced more vocalizations and call types than controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Pairs with T-treated males produced more vocalizations and call types than control pairs.
source: Female mates of T-treated males spent less time at the nest but the pair produced more vocalizations and call types than controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Traditionally, transient T-changes were thought to have transient behavioral effects.
source: Traditionally, transient T-changes were thought to have transient behavioral effects.
evidence: This represents established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: In the wild, when T-pulses occur in a salient context such as a territory, the behavioral effects last days after T-levels return to baseline.
source: Our work demonstrates that in the wild, when T-pulses occur in a salient context such as a territory, the behavioral effects last days after T-levels return to baseline.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing effects lasting multiple days after injections.

claim: Natural male T-pulses occur after social interactions with males or females.
source: We proposed that, as in the laboratory (e.g. Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016), natural male T-pulses occurring after social interactions with males or females would function differently from long-term implants in the field (Fusani, 2008; Goymann et al., 2015; Ketterson et al., 1992; Marler and Moore, 1989; Nyby, 2008) by creating a preference for a specific location within a territory in the wild.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and laboratory studies.

claim: T-pulses function differently from long-term implants in the field by creating a preference for a specific location within a territory.
source: We proposed that, as in the laboratory (e.g. Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016), natural male T-pulses occurring after social interactions with males or females would function differently from long-term implants in the field (Fusani, 2008; Goymann et al., 2015; Ketterson et al., 1992; Marler and Moore, 1989; Nyby, 2008) by creating a preference for a specific location within a territory in the wild.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research and tested in the current study.

claim: T-implants function through classical androgen and estrogen receptors (after conversion to estrogen).
source: One scenario for explaining a possible difference between T-implants and T-pulses is that while T-implants function through classical androgen and estrogen receptors (after conversion to estrogen), the rewarding, possibly more rapid effects, of T can occur through 'nongenomic' actions of androgens (Sato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: The rewarding effects of T can occur through 'nongenomic' actions of androgens.
source: One scenario for explaining a possible difference between T-implants and T-pulses is that while T-implants function through classical androgen and estrogen receptors (after conversion to estrogen), the rewarding, possibly more rapid effects, of T can occur through 'nongenomic' actions of androgens (Sato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: T acts as an internal reward or reinforcing stimulus.
source: T would then act as an internal reward (Gleason et al., 2009) or reinforcing stimulus such that when released naturally or through an injection, increase approach to the physical location in which the T-pulse was experienced, as occurs under laboratory conditions in rodents (e.g. Zhao and Marler, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When T is released naturally or through an injection, it increases approach to the physical location in which the T-pulse was experienced.
source: T would then act as an internal reward (Gleason et al., 2009) or reinforcing stimulus such that when released naturally or through an injection, increase approach to the physical location in which the T-pulse was experienced, as occurs under laboratory conditions in rodents (e.g. Zhao and Marler, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous laboratory research and tested in the current field study.

claim: The reinforcing effects of T occur via activation of the neural internal reward system.
source: The reinforcing effects occur via activation of the neural internal reward system (e.g. Bell and Sisk, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Male T-pulses are released in response to different social interactions across a variety of species including humans.
source: This effect has potentially broad reaching applications because male T-pulses are released in response to different social interactions across a variety of species including humans (Gleason et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: T-release near the nest may provide a mechanism for increasing a male's attendance at the nest for at least several days in a biparental species.
source: In the case of a biparental species, T-release near the nest may provide a mechanism for increasing a male's attendance at the nest for at least several days, as suggested by the results of a laboratory study (Zhao and Marler, 2014) using classical conditioned place preference (CPP) tests (Arnedo et al., 2000; Frye et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous laboratory studies and tested in the current field study.

claim: T has rewarding/reinforcing effects, albeit a weak effect compared to drugs of abuse.
source: We explore the hormone T as a stimulus that has rewarding/reinforcing effects (Arnedo et al., 2000; Frye et al., 2001; Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016; Zhao et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020), albeit a weak effect compared to drugs of abuse (Roozen et al., 2004), in the wild with many relevant, competing stimuli from the natural surrounding environment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The 'Challenge Hypothesis' states that male-male encounters induce increases in T in response to challenges from other males.
source: A classic formalized hypothesis related to T-release in male-male interactions is the 'Challenge Hypothesis' stating that male-male encounters induce increases in T in response to challenges from other males (Wingfield et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a well-established hypothesis in the field supported by citation.

claim: T-pulse release occurs after male-male aggressive encounters in California mice that influence future behavior under laboratory conditions.
source: In a series of laboratory studies in this monogamous, biparental, and highly territorial California mouse (Peromyscus californicus), we found that T-pulse release occurs after male-male aggressive encounters that influence future behavior under laboratory conditions (Gleason et al., 2009; Fuxjager et al., 2011; Marler et al., 2005; Oyegbile and Marler, 2005; Trainor et al., 2004; Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous laboratory studies.

claim: The formation of CPPs can be dependent on the familiarity of the environment and the pair-bond status in California mice.
source: Plasticity in the rewarding nature of these T-pulses has been discovered in this monogamous species, such that the formation of CPPs can be dependent on the familiarity of the environment and the pair-bond status (Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In pair-bonded California mice, T-pulses induce CPPs in familiar but not unfamiliar environments.
source: For example, in pair-bonded California mice, T-pulses induce CPPs in familiar but not unfamiliar environments (Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A male California mouse receiving a T-injection in the middle chamber where he has a nest and is a resident will form a CPP to the nest chamber but not the less familiar side chambers.
source: Specifically, a male receiving a T-injection in the middle chamber where he has a nest and is a resident (increased ability to win a male-male encounter after 24 hr residency) and with his mate temporarily removed (no pups) will form a CPP to the nest chamber but not the less familiar side chambers (Zhao and Marler, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In sexually naïve male California mice, T-pulses induce CPPs in unfamiliar side chambers, but not in familiar environments.
source: Interestingly, the opposite is true for sexually naïve males, in which T-pulses induce CPPs in unfamiliar side chambers, but not in familiar environments (Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The function of T-pulses is dependent on social interactions and location.
source: Therefore, the function of these T-pulses is dependent on social interactions and location.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous findings about CPP formation in different contexts.

claim: T-release occurs in response to female stimuli in California mice.
source: Significantly, T-release occurs in response to female stimuli as well (Zhao and Marler, unpublished data).
evidence: This is supported by unpublished data.

claim: Female stimuli are known to evoke both T-pulses and CPPs from males.
source: Female stimuli are known to evoke both T-pulses (Nyby, 2008; Zhao and Marler unpublished data) and CPPs from males (e.g. Bell et al., 2010; Meisel and Joppa, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and unpublished data.

claim: T and its releasing hormone gonadotropin releasing hormone can have positive effects on paternal behavior in some species.
source: Interestingly, T and its releasing hormone gonadotropin releasing hormone (George et al., 2021) can also have positive effects on paternal behavior in some species (reviewed by Guoynes and Marler, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within minutes of a T-pulse in Gulf toadfish and plainfin midshipman fish, males increased call rate and duration of calls which females prefer.
source: Within minutes of a T-pulse in Gulf toadfish (Opsanus beta) and plainfin midshipman fish (Porichthys notatus), males increased call rate and duration of calls which females prefer (Remage-Healey and Bass, 2004; Remage-Healey and Bass, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Male California mice administered a single T-pulse and placed in the presence of a novel female decreased production of calls associated with courtship in pair-bonded but not unpaired males in the laboratory.
source: Male California mice administered a single T-pulse and placed in the presence of a novel female decreased production of calls associated with courtship in pair-bonded but not unpaired males in the laboratory (Pultorak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Bonding in California mice likely induces a neural change that alters the response to T-pulses and reduces vocal courtship responsiveness to unfamiliar females.
source: This finding indicates that in California mice, bonding likely induces a neural change that alters the response to T-pulses and reduces vocal courtship responsiveness to unfamiliar females (Pultorak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Days after multiple T-pulse injections in the field, male California mice produced more call types with a nonsignificant trend to produce more ultrasonic vocalizations.
source: T-pulses also have long-term effects on call production in California mice, such that days after multiple T-pulse injections in the field, males produced more call types with a nonsignificant trend to produce more ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) (Timonin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pair-bonded males receiving T-injections at the nest would spend more time at the nest.
source: Here, we tested three predictions: (1) pair-bonded males receiving T-injections at the nest would spend more time at the nest;
evidence: This is a prediction that was tested and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: Females would adjust for the increased time that her T-injected mate spent at the nest by decreasing her time at the nest and allocating more time to activities away from the nest.
source: (2) females would adjust for the increased time that her T-injected mate spent at the nest by decreasing her time at the nest and allocating more time to activities away from the nest (based on Trainor and Marler, 2001);
evidence: This is a prediction based on previous research that was tested and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: T-pulses would induce changes in type and number of USVs produced as part of both the direct effects of T on behavior and the indirect effects on the pairs' social adjustment to the altered time allocation to a specific location.
source: (3) T-pulses would induce changes in type and number of USVs produced as part of both the direct effects of T on behavior and the indirect effects on the pairs' social adjustment to the altered time allocation to a specific location (Timonin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction based on previous research that was tested and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: California mice are monogamous and territorial.
source: We tested our hypothesis in the well-studied monogamous and territorial California mouse by administering three T-pulses to paired males at the nest site (Figure 1; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the species.

claim: Male California mice balance their time between behaviors such as mate attendance, offspring care, and territory defense.
source: In this species, males balance their time between behaviors such as mate attendance, offspring care, and territory defense (Gubernick and Alberts, 1987; Gubernick et al., 1993; Gubernick and Teferi, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the laboratory and the wild, California mouse adults frequently produce USVs.
source: In the laboratory and the wild, California mouse adults frequently produce USVs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the species.

claim: In the wild, sustained vocalizations (SVs) and barks are reliably recorded in California mice.
source: In the wild, sustained vocalizations (SVs) and barks are reliably recorded (Briggs and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2011; Kalcounis-Rueppell et al., 2006; Kalcounis-Rueppell et al., 2010; Kalcounis-Rueppell et al., 2018; Timonin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SVs are the most common call type recorded in the field in California mice as single calls or bouts of multiple calls.
source: SVs are the most common call type recorded in the field as single calls or bouts of multiple calls that are categorized based on the number of calls in a bout (1SV, 2SV, 3SV, 4SV; Kalcounis-Rueppell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: SVs are long, low modulation calls with harmonics that may serve as both long-distance contact vocalizations and to convey aggression when in a shortened form.
source: SVs are long, low modulation calls with harmonics that may serve as both long-distance contact vocalizations (Briggs and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2011) and to convey aggression when in a shortened form (Rieger and Marler, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Free-living California mice maintain strict territories.
source: Free-living California mice maintain strict territories (Ribble and Salvioni, 1990), therefore, social interactions at the nest occur primarily between pair members and include production of SVs as is consistent with production of SVs between pairs in the laboratory (Pultorak et al., 2018; Pultorak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Social interactions at the nest in California mice occur primarily between pair members and include production of SVs.
source: Free-living California mice maintain strict territories (Ribble and Salvioni, 1990), therefore, social interactions at the nest occur primarily between pair members and include production of SVs as is consistent with production of SVs between pairs in the laboratory (Pultorak et al., 2018; Pultorak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and logical inference from territorial behavior.

claim: T-males spent 14% more time at the nest than C-males.
source: Overall, T-males spent 14% more time at the nest (defined as within 2 m of the nest) than C-males (GLMM Estimate 0.14 ± 0.05, p = 0.02; Figure 2A; see also Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-females spent 15% less time at the nest than C-females.
source: T-females spent 15% less time at the nest than C-females (GLMM Estimate –0.16 ± 0.06, p = 0.02; Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T- and C-females spent more time at the nest on night three of recording compared to night one of recording.
source: T- and C-females spent more time at the nest on night three of recording compared to night one of recording (night three GLMM Estimate 0.10 ± 0.04, p < 0.02; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-females spent 13% more time at the nest on night three than night one.
source: T-females spent 13% more time at the nest on night three than night one and C-females spent 6% more time on night three than night one (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: C-females spent 6% more time at the nest on night three than night one.
source: T-females spent 13% more time at the nest on night three than night one and C-females spent 6% more time on night three than night one (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Female time at the nest was negatively influenced by male T-injections.
source: Female time at the nest was negatively influenced by male T-injections (T: GLMM Estimate –0.15 ± 0.07, p = 0.04; Supplementary file 1C) and by male time at the nest (Time at the Nest: GLMM Estimate 0.36 ± 0.17, p = 0.04; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Female time at the nest was negatively influenced by male time at the nest.
source: Female time at the nest was negatively influenced by male T-injections (T: GLMM Estimate –0.15 ± 0.07, p = 0.04; Supplementary file 1C) and by male time at the nest (Time at the Nest: GLMM Estimate 0.36 ± 0.17, p = 0.04; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-females spent 5% less time at the nest than their mates.
source: T-females spent 5% less time at the nest than their mates, whereas, C-females spent 18% more time at the nest than their mates (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: C-females spent 18% more time at the nest than their mates.
source: T-females spent 5% less time at the nest than their mates, whereas, C-females spent 18% more time at the nest than their mates (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Males and females spent more time at the nest when there were pups.
source: Males and females spent more time at the nest when there were pups (male time at the nest and pup presences GLMM Estimate –0.21 ± 0.04, p < 0.00; female time at the nest and pup presences GLMM Estimate 0.19 ± 0.06, p < 0.00), however, sample sizes were too small to statistically compare both pup presence and treatment type in one model.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by season.
source: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by season (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.06, p = 0.17), body mass (GLMM Estimate –0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.51), total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.08, p = 0.26) or recording night (comparing night one to night two GLMM Estimate 0.04 ± 0.04, p = 0.39; or night three GLMM Estimate 0.07 ± 0.04, p = 0.11 Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by body mass.
source: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by season (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.06, p = 0.17), body mass (GLMM Estimate –0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.51), total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.08, p = 0.26) or recording night (comparing night one to night two GLMM Estimate 0.04 ± 0.04, p = 0.39; or night three GLMM Estimate 0.07 ± 0.04, p = 0.11 Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by total nights needed to administer all three injections.
source: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by season (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.06, p = 0.17), body mass (GLMM Estimate –0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.51), total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.08, p = 0.26) or recording night (comparing night one to night two GLMM Estimate 0.04 ± 0.04, p = 0.39; or night three GLMM Estimate 0.07 ± 0.04, p = 0.11 Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by recording night.
source: Proportion of male time at the nest was not statistically influenced by season (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.06, p = 0.17), body mass (GLMM Estimate –0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.51), total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.08, p = 0.26) or recording night (comparing night one to night two GLMM Estimate 0.04 ± 0.04, p = 0.39; or night three GLMM Estimate 0.07 ± 0.04, p = 0.11 Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-females spent 15.6% less time in the nest during spring than fall.
source: T-females spent 15.6% less time in the nest during spring than fall (spring GLMM Estimate –0.15 ± 0.06, p = 0.02; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: C-females spent 10.3% less time at the nest during spring than fall.
source: C-females spent 10.3% less time at the nest during spring than fall (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Female time at the nest was not influenced by body mass.
source: Female time at the nest was not, however, influenced by body mass (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.24) or mass difference between the female and the male (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.17).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Female time at the nest was not influenced by mass difference between the female and the male.
source: Female time at the nest was not, however, influenced by body mass (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.24) or mass difference between the female and the male (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.01, p = 0.17).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: A total of 549 total USVs were recorded across the 26 nest sites (T USVs = 368, C USVs = 181).
source: We recorded a total of 549 total USVs across the 26 nest sites (T USVs = 368, C USVs = 181).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data collection.

claim: All call types (1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6SV, and barks) were recorded for the male and the female at both C- and T-nests.
source: All call types (1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6SV, and barks) were recorded for the male and the female at both C- and T-nests.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data collection.

claim: More USVs were produced when two mice were >2 m apart.
source: More USVs were produced when two mice were >2 m apart (χ2 = 9.99, df = 2, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-pairs produced twice as many total USVs at the nest than C-pairs.
source: When considering treatment type, T-pairs produced twice as many total USVs at the nest than C-pairs (GLMM Estimate 0.87 ± .40, p = 0.04; Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Both C- and T-pairs produced twice as many USVs on recording night one than on recording night three.
source: Both C- and T-pairs produced twice as many USVs on recording night one than on recording night three (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Pairs produced more USVs on night one than night three after the last injection.
source: Independent of treatment, additional statistical analyses show that pairs also produced more USVs on night one than night three after the last injection (GLMM Estimate –0.76 ± 0.26, p = 0.01; Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1D), but there was no difference between night one and night two (GLMM Estimate –0.33 ± 0.26, p = 0.15; Figure 3B; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference in USV production between night one and night two.
source: Independent of treatment, additional statistical analyses show that pairs also produced more USVs on night one than night three after the last injection (GLMM Estimate –0.76 ± 0.26, p = 0.01; Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1D), but there was no difference between night one and night two (GLMM Estimate –0.33 ± 0.26, p = 0.15; Figure 3B; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by pups.
source: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by pups (GLMM Estimate –0.48 ± 0.40, p = 0.25), season (GLMM Estimate –0.68 ± 0.40, p = 0.10), body mass (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.06, p = 0.92), or total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.85 ± 0.64, p = 0.20; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by season.
source: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by pups (GLMM Estimate –0.48 ± 0.40, p = 0.25), season (GLMM Estimate –0.68 ± 0.40, p = 0.10), body mass (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.06, p = 0.92), or total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.85 ± 0.64, p = 0.20; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by body mass.
source: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by pups (GLMM Estimate –0.48 ± 0.40, p = 0.25), season (GLMM Estimate –0.68 ± 0.40, p = 0.10), body mass (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.06, p = 0.92), or total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.85 ± 0.64, p = 0.20; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by total nights needed to administer all three injections.
source: The total number of USVs recorded was not influenced by pups (GLMM Estimate –0.48 ± 0.40, p = 0.25), season (GLMM Estimate –0.68 ± 0.40, p = 0.10), body mass (GLMM Estimate 0.01 ± 0.06, p = 0.92), or total nights needed to administer all three injections (GLMM Estimate –0.85 ± 0.64, p = 0.20; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Pairs that spent less time together produced more USVs.
source: When we combined treatments, there was a significant association between the time the pair spent together and USVs (time spent together F2,51 = 20.68, R2 = 0.12, p = 0.03; Figure 4) such that pairs that spent less time together produced more USVs (time spent together F2,51 = 20.68, R2 = 0.12, p = 0.03; treatment p = 0.37; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Male and female mice were more likely to produce SVs when the mate was >2 m from the nest than when located <1 m from the nest.
source: Based on distance alone, both male and female mice were more likely to produce SVs (all SV types combined) when the mate was >2 m from the nest than when located <1 m from the nest (GLM Estimate 0.52 ± 0.12 p < 0.01) and there was a nonsignificant trend for more USVs produced when the mice were 1–2 m apart than <1 m from the nest (GLM Estimate 0.22 ± 0.13, p = 0.09).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was a nonsignificant trend for more USVs produced when the mice were 1–2 m apart than <1 m from the nest.
source: Based on distance alone, both male and female mice were more likely to produce SVs (all SV types combined) when the mate was >2 m from the nest than when located <1 m from the nest (GLM Estimate 0.52 ± 0.12 p < 0.01) and there was a nonsignificant trend for more USVs produced when the mice were 1–2 m apart than <1 m from the nest (GLM Estimate 0.22 ± 0.13, p = 0.09).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was a negative correlation between the number of USVs produced and female time at the nest.
source: There was a negative correlation between the number of USVs produced and female time at the nest (t = −1.96, df = 64, p = 0.05).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-mice were more likely to produce SVs (all types combined) than C-mice.
source: T-mice were more likely to produce SVs (all types combined) than C-mice (treatment GLM Estimate 0.72 ± 0.11 p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-pairs produced proportionately more 4SVs than control pairs.
source: More specifically, when all distances between pair members are combined, T-pairs produced proportionately more 4SVs than control pairs (W = 43, p = 0.03; Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between treatments in any other proportion of call type produced (1-, 2-, 3SV).
source: There was no significant difference between treatments in any other proportion of call type produced (1-, 2-, 3SV; p > 0.137).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: When > 2 m and 1–2 m apart, T-mice were more likely to produce 1-, 2-, and 4SVs.
source: When > 2 m and 1–2 m apart (regardless of pup presence), T-mice were more likely to produce 1-, 2-, and 4SVs (1SVχ2 = 9.95, df = 2, p < 0.01; 2SVχ2 = 9.59, df = 2, p < 0.01; 4SVχ2 = 9.48, df = 2, p < 0.01; Video 1) (again this was not controlled for time pair mates spent together) but not 3SVs (3SVχ2 = 5.1, df = 2, p = 0.08).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: When > 2 m and 1–2 m apart, T-mice were not more likely to produce 3SVs.
source: When > 2 m and 1–2 m apart (regardless of pup presence), T-mice were more likely to produce 1-, 2-, and 4SVs (1SVχ2 = 9.95, df = 2, p < 0.01; 2SVχ2 = 9.59, df = 2, p < 0.01; 4SVχ2 = 9.48, df = 2, p < 0.01; Video 1) (again this was not controlled for time pair mates spent together) but not 3SVs (3SVχ2 = 5.1, df = 2, p = 0.08).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In C-mice there was no significant difference in the proportion of each SV type produced (1–4SVs) for any of the three distances.
source: In C-mice there was no significant difference in the proportion of each SV type produced (1–4SVs) for any of the three distances (p > 0.15).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: T-males produced calls with a 11.25% smaller bandwidth than C-males.
source: There was a treatment effect on call bandwidth, whereby T-males produced calls with a 11.25% smaller bandwidth than C-males (GLM Estimate –0.13 ± 0.01, p < 0.01; Figure 5; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no treatment effect on other spectral or temporal characteristics of calls in males.
source: There was, however, no effect on other spectral or temporal characteristics of calls (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference between treatment types in call duration for males.
source: There was no difference between treatment types in call duration (GLM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.12, p = 0.46) or PC1 score (GLM Estimate 0.77 ± 1.07, p = 0.48; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference between treatment types in PC1 score for males.
source: There was no difference between treatment types in call duration (GLM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.12, p = 0.46) or PC1 score (GLM Estimate 0.77 ± 1.07, p = 0.48; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: For females, there was no significant difference between treatment type and any call characteristics, duration, bandwidth, or PC1 score.
source: For females, there was no significant difference between treatment type and any call characteristics, duration (GLM Estimate –0.09 ± 0.21, p = 0.68), bandwidth (GLM Estimate –0.11 ± 0.07, p = 0.88), or PC1 score (GLM Estimate 0.51 ± 1.02, p = 0.63; Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: This is the first field study that demonstrates a potentially natural function of transient T-pulses, that of inducing place preferences, possibly through CPPs.
source: In summary, this is the first field study that demonstrates a potentially natural function of transient T-pulses, that of inducing place preferences, possibly through CPPs.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty and significance of the study's findings.

claim: T-pulses naturally occur in a variety of different species, including humans.
source: T-pulses naturally occur in a variety of different species, including humans (review by Fuxjager et al., 2017), and our results are consistent with other research in which T-pulses have rewarding properties and can condition animals to the physical location in which the hormone release occurred (e.g. Arnedo et al., 2000; Frye et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Despite T being weakly reinforcing compared to many drugs, it can alter behavior in a complex natural environment.
source: We now know that despite T being weakly reinforcing compared to many drugs, it can alter behavior and do so in a complex natural environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The change in the allocation of time spent in specific physical environments is associated with changes in call production.
source: This change in the allocation of time spent in specific physical environments is also associated with changes in call production, likely resulting, in part, from T-induced changes in social interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: When T altered male time spent at the nest, it may have resulted in increased paternal behavior, and a compensatory decrease in maternal behavior.
source: When T altered male time spent at the nest, it may also have resulted in increased paternal behavior, and a compensatory decrease in maternal behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: There could be an adaptive significance for a co-option mechanism that allows a close association between mating release of T and paternal behavior.
source: We speculate that there could be an adaptive significance for a co-option mechanism that allows a close association between mating release of T and paternal behavior.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: T-pulses are tied in with active learning from a changing social environment during the breeding season in relation to functions related to reproduction.
source: We speculate, however, that the T-pulses are tied in with active learning from a changing social environment during the breeding season in relation to functions related to reproduction.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: T-pulses have the potential to allow males to adjust to changing social conditions in the wild through both spatial preference and vocal plasticity of a male and his mate.
source: Once thought to be of little importance, especially in humans (Geniole et al., 2020), we are discovering that T-pulses have the potential to allow males to adjust to changing social conditions in the wild through both spatial preference and vocal plasticity of a male and his mate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and supported by citation.

claim: Field work was conducted at the Hastings Natural History Reservation, Carmel Valley, CA, USA, from January to June 2015 (spring) and from September to December 2015 (fall).
source: Field work was conducted at the Hastings Natural History Reservation (HNHR), Carmel Valley, CA, USA, from January to June 2015 (spring) and from September to December 2015 (fall) on established trapping grids.
evidence: This is a description of the study methods.

claim: The study had 169,222 trap nights over 211 nights.
source: Our methods include high trapping efforts to ensure a high probability of capture for all resident individuals at our study site; in this study we had 169,222 trap nights over 211 nights that include pre-experiment and experiment nights.
evidence: This is a description of the study methods.

claim: An average of 1500 m2 territory size has been recorded for California mice.
source: For California mice, an average of 1500 m2 territory size has been recorded (MacMillen, 1964); we studied their behaviors at the nest and the 2 m area immediately around the nest.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Of the 323 mice tagged, 33 reproductively active mated pairs were identified.
source: Of the 323 mice tagged, we identified 33 reproductively active mated pairs (males with enlarged testis and females were pregnant and/or lactating).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The dose of T-injection was approximately 36 μg/kg (T-cyclodextrin dissolved in saline) which mimics natural T-pulses.
source: The dose of T-injection was approximately 36 μg/kg (T-cyclodextrin dissolved in saline) which mimics natural T-pulses (Oyegbile and Marler, 2005; Trainor et al., 2004) and has been used successfully in multiple California mouse studies primarily focused on aggression and courtship (Fuxjager et al., 2011; Pultorak et al., 2015; Timonin et al., 2018; Trainor et al., 2004; Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the study methods supported by citations to previous research.

claim: T-implants cause increases in territorial patrolling in the mountain spiny lizard, Sceloporus jarrovi.
source: For example, T-implants cause increases in territorial patrolling in the mountain spiny lizard, Sceloporus jarrovi (Marler and Moore, 1989), larger home ranges and territories in both avian and lizard species (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997; DeNardo and Sinervo, 1994; Watson and Parr, 1981; Wingfield, 1984), decreased paternal care in the form of time at the nest (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997), and increased singing in birds (review by Lynn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: T-implants cause larger home ranges and territories in both avian and lizard species.
source: For example, T-implants cause increases in territorial patrolling in the mountain spiny lizard, Sceloporus jarrovi (Marler and Moore, 1989), larger home ranges and territories in both avian and lizard species (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997; DeNardo and Sinervo, 1994; Watson and Parr, 1981; Wingfield, 1984), decreased paternal care in the form of time at the nest (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997), and increased singing in birds (review by Lynn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: T-implants cause decreased paternal care in the form of time at the nest.
source: For example, T-implants cause increases in territorial patrolling in the mountain spiny lizard, Sceloporus jarrovi (Marler and Moore, 1989), larger home ranges and territories in both avian and lizard species (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997; DeNardo and Sinervo, 1994; Watson and Parr, 1981; Wingfield, 1984), decreased paternal care in the form of time at the nest (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997), and increased singing in birds (review by Lynn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: T-implants cause increased singing in birds.
source: For example, T-implants cause increases in territorial patrolling in the mountain spiny lizard, Sceloporus jarrovi (Marler and Moore, 1989), larger home ranges and territories in both avian and lizard species (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997; DeNardo and Sinervo, 1994; Watson and Parr, 1981; Wingfield, 1984), decreased paternal care in the form of time at the nest (e.g. Chandler et al., 1997), and increased singing in birds (review by Lynn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Castration resulted in fewer songs in male singing mice.
source: Within rodents, long-term androgen manipulations in the laboratory can also alter vocalizations; for example, Pasch et al., 2011a found that castration resulted in fewer songs in male singing mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The increase in songs of male singing mice in response to T appears to function directly in male-male aggression.
source: In contrast, the increase in songs of male singing mice in response to T appears to function directly in male-male aggression (Pasch et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Blocking T conversion to estradiol influences effects of baseline levels of T on aggression in the form of attack latency in California mice, but not the T-pulses that mimic experience-induced aggression.
source: First, within California mice it is known that blocking T conversion to estradiol influences effects of baseline levels of T on aggression in the form of attack latency, but not the T-pulses that mimic experience-induced aggression; this suggests that baseline effects of T on aggression are related to estrogen receptors, and experience-induced effects are related to androgen receptors (Trainor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Baseline effects of T on aggression are related to estrogen receptors, and experience-induced effects are related to androgen receptors in California mice.
source: First, within California mice it is known that blocking T conversion to estradiol influences effects of baseline levels of T on aggression in the form of attack latency, but not the T-pulses that mimic experience-induced aggression; this suggests that baseline effects of T on aggression are related to estrogen receptors, and experience-induced effects are related to androgen receptors (Trainor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Androgen reinforcement can act through membrane androgen receptors and/or androgen metabolites.
source: The rewarding/reinforcing effects of T-pulses may well operate through other proposed cellular mechanisms; androgen reinforcement can act through membrane androgen receptors (Wood, 2004) and/or androgen metabolites (e.g. Frye, 2007; Rosellini et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: T-pulses may provide another neuroendocrine mechanism for allowing males to avoid the high costs of sustained T-levels characterized by decreased survivorship or condition.
source: Two other broad concepts to emphasize are first that T-pulses may provide another neuroendocrine mechanism for allowing males to avoid the high costs of sustained T-levels characterized by decreased survivorship or condition (e.g. Alonso-Alvarez et al., 2007; Buchanan et al., 2001; Dufty, 1989; Fuxjager et al., 2011; Sinervo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Conditioning via T-pulses supports the concept that T-pulses are another mechanism for altering androgen-influenced phenotypes.
source: Moreover, conditioning via T-pulses further supports the concept that T-pulses are another mechanism for altering androgen-influenced phenotypes, albeit probably more transient in nature (review by Fuxjager and Schuppe, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The CPP behavioral paradigm is used extensively in laboratory studies for measuring the reinforcing and addictive nature of drugs and neurochemicals.
source: Second, from a laboratory perspective, we found evidence consistent with the concept that the weak conditioning effects of T-pulses via CPPs can increase time allocation by a mammal to a location, the nest, within a territory in the wild. The CPP behavioral paradigm is used extensively in laboratory studies for measuring the reinforcing and addictive nature of drugs and neurochemicals, but there is a gap in our understanding of the natural functions for these location preferences, including the relatively weak effects produced by T.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CPP paradigm.

claim: There is a gap in our understanding of the natural functions for location preferences, including the relatively weak effects produced by T.
source: The CPP behavioral paradigm is used extensively in laboratory studies for measuring the reinforcing and addictive nature of drugs and neurochemicals, but there is a gap in our understanding of the natural functions for these location preferences, including the relatively weak effects produced by T.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: T-injections in the laboratory can alter both time spent in a location and social behaviors in California mice.
source: In the context of CPPs, we previously found that these injections in the laboratory can alter both time spent in a location (Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016) and social behaviors (Fuxjager et al., 2011; Pultorak et al., 2015; Trainor et al., 2004; Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: T-pulses have reinforcing/rewarding effects as described in mice, rats, and hamsters.
source: Our results are consistent with laboratory observations in mice, rats, and hamsters showing that T-pulses have reinforcing/rewarding effects as described in the introduction (Alexander et al., 1994; Arnedo et al., 2000; Wood, 2004; Zhao and Marler, 2014; Zhao and Marler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Androgen-induced CPPs can be blocked by dopamine antagonists.
source: It is of interest to note that the androgen-induced CPPs can be blocked by dopamine antagonists (Becker and Marler, 2015), further supporting the concept of reinforcing/reward functions (Gleason et al., 2009; Marler et al., 2005; Packard et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The importance of the male-female interaction in eliciting T-pulses across species has been highlighted by Goymann et al., 2019.
source: The importance of the male-female interaction in eliciting T-pulses across species has been highlighted by Goymann et al., 2019.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Male mice and rats exposed to an estrous female or her olfactory cues show a preference for the location at which the sexual encounter occurred.
source: Male mice and rats exposed to an estrous female or her olfactory cues show a preference for the location at which the sexual encounter occurred (Camacho et al., 2004; Frye et al., 2001; Hughes et al., 1990; Mehrara and Baum, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased T causes males to allocate more time toward mate guarding, courting, or aggressively pursuing other males based on the knowledge of functions of T.
source: Based on the knowledge of functions of T, one might predict that increased T causes males to allocate more time toward mate guarding, courting, or aggressively pursuing other males.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established knowledge about T functions.

claim: The change in spatial preference in the current study was most likely not a result of behavioral changes other than the T-induced CPPs.
source: In the current study, however, the change in spatial preference was most likely not a result of behavioral changes other than the T-induced CPPs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: There was no evidence for increased mate guarding behavior in the current study since females spent more time away from the nest while males spent more time at the nest.
source: We found no evidence for increased mate guarding behavior since females spent more time away from the nest while males spent more time at the nest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The administration of a single T-pulse caused paired but not unpaired male California mice to decrease sweep USVs to unfamiliar females in the laboratory.
source: This lack of increased sexual behavior to unfamiliar females is also consistent with the finding that the administration of a single T-pulse caused paired but not unpaired male California mice to decrease sweep USVs to unfamiliar females in the laboratory (Pultorak et al., 2015), suggesting a dampening of the classical increase in vocalizations that occurs in response to the combined stimulus of T and the presence of a female in rodents (review by Marler and Monari, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There was no evidence in the current study that T-pulses increased aggression.
source: In the context of the nest site, there was no evidence in the current study that T-pulses increased aggression (see laboratory studies focused on male-male interactions; Marler and Trainor, 2020), as evidenced by lack of injuries (all animals tested were trapped post experiment with no visible injuries) or increase in aggressive barks or shortening of SV calls (Supplementary file 1G; see Pultorak et al., 2018, for evidence that barks can be produced in male-female interactions).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings supported by citations.

claim: Males may have been actively pushing females out of the nest as has been anecdotally observed in laboratory situations by either sex when challenged by an intruder.
source: We cannot, however, rule out that males may have been actively pushing females out of the nest as has been anecdotally observed in laboratory situations by either sex when challenged by an intruder (Rieger and Marler, unpublished data).
evidence: This is speculation based on unpublished observations.

claim: The most likely explanation for what males were doing at the nest is increased paternal behavior in the form of increased nest defense or paternal care of pups.
source: What then were males doing at the nest? In this case, the most likely explanation is increased paternal behavior (when pups were at the nest) in the form of increased nest defense or paternal care of pups based on evidence, described below, that T can directly increase paternal care in California mice in the laboratory or possibly as a by-product of spending more time at the nest.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and previous research.

claim: T increases the focus on the reproductive or aggressive behaviors most relevant at that time depending on the social and physical contexts for that specific species.
source: We suggest that T increases the focus on the reproductive or aggressive behaviors most relevant at that time depending on the social and physical contexts for that specific species (Hurley and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2018).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the study's findings and supported by citation.

claim: The ability to create T-induced conditioned location preferences is plastic and varies with social experience and current social and physical contexts.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that the ability to create T-induced conditioned location preferences is plastic and varies with social experience and current social and physical (e.g. familiar versus unfamiliar locations) contexts (Zhao and Marler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: T-pulse release following a sexual encounter most likely occurs at the nest site in nature.
source: In nature, T-pulse release following a sexual encounter most likely occurs at the nest site (as is characteristic of rodents) when females first approach a male that has established a territory.
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge of rodent behavior.

claim: T-pulses are expected to occur when the female is in postpartum estrus.
source: In addition, T-pulses are expected to occur when the female is in postpartum estrus (Gubernick and Nelson, 1989).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: T-induced CPPs could be the mechanism for increasing paternal care indirectly through increased preference for spending time at the nest.
source: Therefore, T-induced CPPs could be the mechanism for increasing paternal care indirectly through increased preference for spending time at the nest.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: T can promote paternal care in male California mice and other species.
source: In addition, T can promote paternal care in male California mice and other species (e.g. Juana et al., 2010; Luis et al., 2013; Ziegler et al., 2004); although this is variable among species (review by Hirschenhauser et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: California mouse pups demand extensive paternal investment because they are altricial and exothermic and depend on adult presence to maintain their body temperature.
source: California mouse pups demand extensive paternal investment because they are altricial and exothermic and depend on adult presence to maintain their body temperature (Gubernick and Alberts, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the California mouse, the presence of the father has a significant positive effect on offspring survival when temperatures are low and the parents have to forage, but there is no effect of father's presence on pup survival when exposed to warm temperatures in the laboratory.
source: In the California mouse, the presence of the father has a significant positive effect on offspring survival when temperatures are low and the parents have to forage, but there is no effect of father's presence on pup survival when exposed to warm temperatures in the laboratory (Gubernick et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Paternal presence has a significant positive effect on offspring survival in the field in California mice.
source: The importance of the father, however, is highlighted by findings in the wild that paternal presence has a significant positive effect on offspring survival in the field (Gubernick and Teferi, 2000), and in laboratory studies (Bambico et al., 2013; Cantoni and Brown, 1997; Rosenfeld et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The main limiting factor in California mouse reproduction is water availability.
source: The main limiting factor in California mouse reproduction is water availability (Nelson et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In some biparental species, T-induced CPPs could be a mechanism for keeping the male at the nest to care for the young while the female forages or conducts other behaviors related to territory maintenance.
source: We, therefore, propose that in some biparental species, T-induced CPPs could be a mechanism for keeping the male at the nest to care for the young while the female forages or conducts other behaviors related to territory maintenance.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the study's findings.

claim: Females are territorial and aggressive and also actively approach intruders or playbacks of intruders of both sexes in California mice.
source: Females are territorial and aggressive and also actively approach intruders or playbacks of intruders of both sexes (e.g. Davis and Marler, 2003; Davis and Marler, 2004; Rieger and Marler, 2018; Rieger et al., 2019; Rieger et al., 2021; Monari et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Another selection pressure for T-induced paternal behavior may be increased protectiveness of pups to prevent the high levels of conspecific infanticide found in rodents.
source: Another selection pressure for T-induced paternal behavior may be increased protectiveness of pups to prevent the high levels of conspecific infanticide found in rodents (Agrell et al., 1998).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: van Anders et al., 2012 speculate that infant protection may be positively associated with T and more nurturing behaviors negatively associated with T.
source: van Anders et al., 2012 speculate that infant protection may be positively associated with T and more nurturing behaviors negatively associated with T.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The reinforcing effects of T-pulses may function to allocate more time in the familiar environment and display behaviors that have direct fitness benefits.
source: In summary, the reinforcing effects of T-pulses may function to allocate more time in the familiar environment and display behaviors that have direct fitness benefits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: One possibility for why females changed their spatial preference to be away from the nest is to compensate for the T-induced changes in male spatial preferences.
source: One possibility for why females changed their spatial preference to be away from the nest is to compensate for the T-induced changes in male spatial preferences.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: A reduction in paternal behavior is associated with an increase in maternal huddling behavior in California mice in laboratory studies.
source: This is consistent with laboratory studies finding that a reduction in paternal behavior is associated with an increase in maternal huddling behavior (Trainor and Marler, 2001), although no compensation was found in other California mouse studies (review by Bester-Meredith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Results regarding maternal compensation for paternal behavior are varied in prairie voles.
source: Results are varied in prairie voles as well (Ahern et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: This is the first field study to indirectly test the idea of maternal adjustment for level of paternal care.
source: Ours is the first field study to indirectly test this idea of maternal adjustment for level of paternal care.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Plasticity in male time at the nest is influenced by T from social stimuli, whereas the plasticity in female time at the nest may be influenced more directly by the physical environment.
source: We speculate that plasticity in the males is influenced by T from social stimuli, whereas the plasticity we see in the females may be influenced more directly by the physical environment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: In species that form pair-bonds where both members of a pair are engaged in offspring care and territory defense, the delegation of tasks is beneficial.
source: In species that form pair-bonds where both members of a pair are engaged in offspring care and territory defense, the delegation of tasks is beneficial.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of cooperative breeding.

claim: In a wider variety of taxonomic groups, including insects, birds, fish, and mammals that engage in cooperative breeding, members of a pair or group often distribute tasks.
source: In a wider variety of taxonomic groups, including insects, birds, fish, and mammals that engage in cooperative breeding, members of a pair or group often distribute tasks (Arnold et al., 2005; Ahern et al., 2011; Mathews, 2002; Page et al., 2006; Quinard and Cézilly, 2012; Rieger et al., 2019; Rogers, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When challenged with a potential intruder in the laboratory, California mouse pairs either coordinate their behavior in joint defense or employ labor division strategies.
source: In the laboratory, when challenged with a potential intruder, California mouse pairs either coordinate their behavior in joint defense or employ labor division strategies, with the latter strategy potentially more likely to occur after pups are born (Rieger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the California mouse, when the male is present but decreases paternal care due to castration, the female compensates for her mate's behavior by increasing huddling with her pups.
source: In the California mouse, when the male is present but decreases paternal care due to castration, the female compensates for her mate's behavior by increasing huddling with her pups (Trainor and Marler, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In species in which both members provide offspring care, such as in the Midas cichlid, great tit, and prairie vole, the presence of offspring increases the pairs' use of division of labor.
source: In species in which both members provide offspring care, such as in the Midas cichlid, great tit, and prairie vole, the presence of offspring increases the pairs' use of division of labor (Rogers, 1988; Ahern et al., 2011; Boucaud et al., 2016; Rogers et al., 2018; ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Division of labor can have important long-term benefits for the persistence and survival of a social group.
source: This division of labor can have important long-term benefits for the persistence and survival of a social group (Arnold et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: If the male is spending more time in one location, such as the nest to care for offspring, the female is adjusting her space use by allocating more time to other parts of the territory, such as foraging and/or defending the territory against potential intruders.
source: In the case of California mice, if the male is spending more time in one location, such as the nest to care for offspring, the female is adjusting her space use by allocating more time to other parts of the territory, such as foraging and/or defending the territory against potential intruders.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: T-pulses can alter space use and females can adjust their behavior to compensate for male changes in space use.
source: These results suggest that T-pulses can alter space use and, importantly, females can adjust their behavior to compensate for male changes in space use.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The same transient increases in T that induced CPPs also had long-term effects (>24 hr) on vocal communication by increasing the number of USVs produced and altering both the type of calls produced and the call bandwidth.
source: We also found that the same transient increases in T that induced CPPs also had long-term effects (>24 hr) on vocal communication by increasing the number of USVs produced and altering both the type of calls produced and the call bandwidth.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Timonin et al., 2018 found a nonsignificant trend for a positive effect of T-pulses on USVs in California mice in the wild.
source: Our results are consistent with these other studies and Timonin et al., 2018, also found a nonsignificant trend for a positive effect of T-pulses on USVs in California mice in the wild.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Timonin et al., 2018 found that T-pairs produced proportionately more 1-, 4-, and 5SVs, whereas the current study only found an effect on 4SVs.
source: One difference between the studies is that Timonin et al., 2018 found that T-pairs produced proportionately more 1-, 4-, and 5SVs, whereas we only found an effect on 4SVs.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings across studies.

claim: The difference between the Timonin study and the current study could be attributed to year, population densities, or a higher sample size in the current study.
source: The difference between the Timonin study and the current study could be attributed to year, population densities, or a higher sample size in the current study.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for differences between studies.

claim: At least 4SVs are being used to communicate between spatially separated pairs.
source: We speculate that at least 4SVs are being used to communicate between spatially separated pairs, as suggested by Briggs and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2011.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The increased time apart in T-pairs may indirectly drive the greater number of USVs produced by the T-pairs.
source: The current study also reveals that the increased time apart in T-pairs may indirectly drive the greater number of USVs produced by the T-pairs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Narrow bandwidth SVs may be more efficient for longer distance communication as narrow bandwidth USVs are less susceptible to environmental degradation and may travel further.
source: Narrow bandwidth SVs may be more efficient for longer distance communication as narrow bandwidth USVs are less susceptible to environmental degradation and may travel further (Barber et al., 2010; Slabbekoorn, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In golden hamsters, T-pulses increased bandwidth of calls produced in close proximity.
source: Contrary to our findings that T-pulses decreased bandwidth in SVs, in the golden hamsters (Mesocricetus auratus) T-pulses increased bandwidth of calls, but these were produced in close proximity (Fernández-Vargas, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Singing mice administered T-implants produced mating calls with increased bandwidth, which females tended to prefer.
source: Singing mice (Scotinomys teguina) administered T-implants produced mating calls also with increased bandwidth, which females tended to prefer (Pasch et al., 2011a; Pasch et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: California mice may not follow the same pattern of call production as in golden hamsters and singing mice because they are likely directing SV calls toward the other member of the already established pair.
source: We speculate that under the conditions of male-female interactions in a mate-choice context, the function of the bandwidth change may be related to the increased call complexity and greater information transfer characteristic of wider bandwidths. California mice may not follow the same pattern of call production as in golden hamsters and singing mice because in our study they are likely directing SV calls toward the other member of the already established pair (Briggs and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Offspring presence did not influence call production in the current study.
source: Moreover, calls are unlikely to be directed toward pups because in the current study offspring presence did not influence call production.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The calls may serve a dual function, as mate contact calls and/or as territorial advertisement.
source: It is also possible, however, and remains untested, that the calls serve a dual function, as mate contact calls and/or as territorial advertisement.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of calls.

claim: Call production most likely serves to at least maintain awareness of the other individuals in a complex environment.
source: Call production most likely serves to at least maintain awareness of the other individuals in a complex environment (Hurley and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.
